promptText: Of the three observability pillars, which one is best suited to answering 'why did this one specific request fail'?
options: Logs - discrete, high-detail events like a stack trace or exception reason
Metrics - aggregated numeric measurements across the whole fleet
Traces alone, without any logs, since spans always contain the error reason
None of them - you would need to reproduce the failure locally
explanation: Metrics are aggregated and cheap but throw away per-request detail, so they answer 'what/how much'; traces show where time went across services; logs are the richest source of 'why' for one specific event, which is why the standard workflow uses a metric to spot a problem, a trace to localize it, and logs for the exact reason.

promptText: A team wants to track the current depth of an in-memory queue, which can increase or decrease as items are added and processed. Which Micrometer meter type is correct?
options: Gauge - it reports a point-in-time value that can go up or down
Counter - it should be incremented on enqueue and decremented on dequeue
Timer - it measures how long each item stays in the queue
DistributionSummary - it tracks the total number of items ever enqueued
explanation: A Counter only ever increases (or resets on restart) and is for counting occurrences; a value that can legitimately go up or down, like current queue depth, must be a Gauge, since wrapping a decreasing value in a Counter makes it impossible to see the current state.

promptText: Where should a check for database connectivity be wired in - Kubernetes liveness or readiness probe - and why?
options: Readiness, so a transient DB blip only removes the pod from traffic routing without restarting it
Liveness, so a transient DB blip triggers an immediate restart of the pod
Either one works identically since both trigger the same remediation
Neither - database checks should never appear in any Kubernetes probe
explanation: If a downstream dependency check is wired into liveness instead of readiness, a transient database blip causes Kubernetes to restart every replica simultaneously, which does nothing to fix the database and destroys the warm instance pool - readiness simply pulls the pod from rotation until the dependency recovers, then adds it back.

promptText: How does an SLA typically relate to a service's internal SLO?
options: The SLA is usually set looser than the internal SLO, so missing the SLO still leaves room to fix things before breaching the customer-facing SLA
The SLA is always identical to the SLO since both represent the same measured value
The SLA is stricter than the SLO because it is legally binding
SLAs and SLOs are unrelated concepts measuring completely different systems
explanation: An SLO is the internal target for an SLI, while an SLA is an external, usually contractual commitment typically set looser than the SLO with real financial consequences for missing it - this gap gives the team room to notice and fix a slipping SLO before it becomes an SLA breach.

promptText: Which Spring Boot Actuator endpoint should a Prometheus scrape_configs entry point at?
options: /actuator/prometheus - built for scheduled scraping in the Prometheus exposition format
/actuator/metrics - the generic, human-browsable listing endpoint
/actuator/health - the aggregated UP/DOWN status endpoint
/actuator/info - static build and version metadata
explanation: /actuator/metrics is meant for ad hoc interactive inspection of individual meters, not high-frequency polling; /actuator/prometheus requires micrometer-registry-prometheus and serves every meter in the Prometheus text exposition format in one response, which is what a scrape config must target.

promptText: A service has an SLO of 99.9% availability over a rolling 28-day window. Roughly how much error budget does that leave?
options: About 0.1% of the period, roughly 40 minutes of downtime-equivalent over 28 days
Exactly zero, since 99.9% means no failures are ever tolerated
50% of the period, since error budgets are always half of the SLO
It cannot be calculated without knowing the SLA as well
explanation: The error budget is simply 100% minus the SLO turned into a spendable allowance; at 99.9% the budget is 0.1% of the period, which over a 28-day window works out to roughly 40 minutes of full downtime-equivalent that the team can spend on releases and calculated risk.

promptText: How does 'observability' differ from classic 'monitoring' in the known-unknowns vs unknown-unknowns framing?
options: Monitoring watches for anticipated failure modes with predefined thresholds; observability lets you explore high-cardinality telemetry to answer questions about failure modes nobody predicted in advance
Monitoring and observability are simply two marketing terms for the exact same practice with no functional difference
Observability only refers to having a Grafana dashboard, while monitoring refers to having any alert at all
Monitoring is for logs and observability is for metrics - they cover different pillars entirely
explanation: Monitoring answers questions you thought to ask in advance (known-unknowns) via static dashboards and threshold alerts, while observability is a property of the system that lets you infer internal state and slice arbitrary high-cardinality data to investigate a question you never wrote a dashboard for (unknown-unknowns) - the two are complementary, not interchangeable.

promptText: Why is querying rate() over a Prometheus counter almost always necessary instead of reading the counter's raw value directly?
options: A raw counter is a cumulative total that only ever grows, so rate() is what computes how fast it's actually increasing per second, correctly handling resets like a pod restart
rate() is required because Prometheus counters are stored as strings and must be parsed into numbers first
The raw value of a counter resets to zero every scrape interval, so it is meaningless without rate()
rate() converts a counter into a gauge type, which is the only type Grafana can graph
explanation: Counters are cumulative totals since the process started, which is almost never the useful number directly - rate() computes the per-second speed of increase over a sliding window and correctly handles counter resets (such as on a restart), which is why it appears in nearly every real dashboard query.

promptText: Why can't you correctly compute an overall p99 latency by simply averaging the p99 values reported independently by each of 10 service instances?
options: Percentiles do not average meaningfully - you must aggregate at the histogram-bucket level first (sum by le) and only then compute the quantile
Averaging is fine for p99 but not for p50 or p95, which behave completely differently
Prometheus physically disallows the AVG function from being applied to any metric with 'seconds' in its name
Each instance's p99 is always identical in a correctly load-balanced system, making the question moot
explanation: A p99 of 100ms on one instance and 300ms on another is not a p99 of 200ms across both - percentiles cannot be meaningfully averaged after the fact; histogram_quantile() requires summing the underlying bucket counts across instances first and only then computing the quantile from the combined histogram.

promptText: What is the fundamental trade-off between head-based and tail-based trace sampling?
options: Head-based decides blind at the start of a request and is cheap; tail-based waits until a trace completes so it can guarantee errors and slow requests are always kept, at the cost of buffering and added latency
Head-based can only sample synchronous HTTP calls, while tail-based works only for asynchronous message-queue calls
Tail-based sampling is always cheaper than head-based because it discards more traces overall
Head-based sampling guarantees every error is captured, while tail-based sampling captures errors only by chance
explanation: Head-based sampling makes the keep/drop decision at the root span before the outcome is known, so it cannot selectively keep errors or slow requests; tail-based sampling buffers all of a trace's spans until it finishes and applies policies like 'always keep errors,' guaranteeing high-value traces are never dropped, but requiring all of a trace's spans to reach the same collector and adding buffering overhead.

promptText: An engineer adds a raw user id as a label on a frequently-recorded business metric. Why is this dangerous for a shared Prometheus deployment?
options: Prometheus allocates a distinct time series per unique label-value combination, so an unbounded label like a raw user id can generate millions of series, exhausting memory on the shared metrics server
Prometheus rejects any label value containing non-numeric characters, causing the application to crash on startup
Labels with user data are automatically stripped by Prometheus, silently corrupting the metric
This only affects the single dashboard using that metric and cannot impact anything else in the deployment
explanation: Cardinality is the number of unique label-value combinations a metric can take, and each combination gets its own in-memory time series; an unbounded label like a raw user id or an un-templated path can create millions of series, and this typically surfaces as generic memory pressure or an OOM on the metrics server rather than an obvious error at the call site that caused it.

promptText: What is the core architectural trade-off Grafana Loki makes compared to an ELK/EFK stack for log aggregation?
options: Loki indexes only a small set of labels and stores raw log content unindexed in object storage, making it far cheaper but weaker at ad hoc full-text search than Elasticsearch's full-field indexing
Loki and Elasticsearch use an identical indexing strategy, differing only in their choice of UI (Grafana vs Kibana)
Loki cannot store logs from Kubernetes at all and is only usable for VM-based deployments
Elasticsearch is cheaper than Loki because it compresses data more aggressively before indexing
explanation: Elasticsearch fully indexes every field of every log line for powerful ad hoc search at significant CPU/storage cost; Loki, modeled on Prometheus's own approach, indexes only a bounded set of labels and greps the compressed, unindexed content within an already-narrowed stream, trading full-text search power for dramatically lower cost at scale.

promptText: Why does mature burn-rate alerting evaluate the error-budget consumption ratio over multiple time windows (e.g. both 1 hour and 6 hours) rather than a single flat threshold?
options: A single window either misses slow, sustained degradations or pages on every brief spike; evaluating short and long windows together catches both a severe short burn and a milder longer burn at appropriately different urgency
Multiple windows are required because Prometheus cannot evaluate any alert rule over a period longer than one hour
A single window would always exhaust the entire error budget instantly regardless of actual error rate
Grafana requires at least two overlapping time windows before it will render any alert panel at all
explanation: A burn-rate value of 1 means the budget is being consumed exactly on pace, and 10 means ten times faster than sustainable; using Google's multi-window multi-burn-rate approach (e.g. 1h and 6h simultaneously) lets a short severe spike page immediately while a longer mild degradation is caught without either scenario being missed or causing excessive noise from a single flat threshold.

promptText: During an incident, a golden-signal dashboard shows checkout's p99 latency doubled at 14:02. What is the correct next step in the metrics-to-trace-to-log workflow, and what specifically enables jumping from the metric straight to a relevant trace?
options: Filter traces for checkout's root span during that window to find the dominant slow downstream call, then pull logs for that trace id; exemplars attached to the latency histogram let you click directly from a slow bucket to one concrete trace
Immediately restart the checkout service, since a p99 spike always indicates a memory leak requiring a restart
Increase the sampling rate to 100% permanently so all future incidents are pre-diagnosed
Average the p99 values from all checkout instances to compute which one is at fault
explanation: The metric tells you something is wrong and roughly when; filtering traces for that window narrows down where the time is going (e.g. a specific downstream call taking far longer than usual); logs filtered by those trace ids reveal why. Exemplars are the concrete Prometheus/OpenMetrics mechanism attaching a trace id to an individual histogram observation, letting Grafana render clickable points on a latency panel that jump straight into one specific trace.

promptText: A heap-used gauge trends steadily upward over days without returning to baseline after garbage collections, and GC pause duration is climbing. What can observability metrics alone tell you, and what additional tool is required to actually find the root cause?
options: Metrics can localize the timeframe the leak started and which instance is affected, but identifying which specific object graph is leaking requires capturing and analyzing an actual heap dump with a profiler
Metrics alone are always sufficient to identify the exact leaking class without any further tooling
GC pause duration climbing means the JVM will automatically fix the leak by triggering a full compaction
A rising heap-used gauge with no sawtooth pattern indicates a networking issue, not a memory leak, and should be diagnosed with tcpdump instead
explanation: The saturation golden signal (heap trending up without the normal post-GC sawtooth) detects and localizes when and where a leak is happening, and rising GC pause times explain the resulting latency and eventual OutOfMemoryError - but metrics structurally cannot identify which object graph is leaking, which requires an actual heap dump (via a secured /actuator/heapdump or jmap) analyzed offline with a profiler.
